risks: Minimal physical risk. The main risks are that a low score becomes a label, that managers learn individual scores, and that residents feel surveilled; scores never leave the residency office and are not used for performance or employment decisions.
consent: Verbal consent at the month-3 seminar after a short information sheet that states who sees the score, what human resources shares, and that declining changes nothing about the residency; consent can be withdrawn until the 12-month extract.
data: Study numbers link scores and dates; the name key is held only by the residency office; the analysis file holds no names, no unit and no manager; files are kept on the hospital research drive and destroyed five years after publication.
equity: PROGRESS-Plus: residents who are first in their family to attend university, internationally raised graduates, residents with caring responsibilities and those on night-heavy rotations or at the rural campus may experience transition differently. Accuracy is reported descriptively for these groups, and the booster, if built, is offered on request to anyone regardless of score.
effectiveness: The study succeeds if it gives a local estimate precise enough to decide whether the cut-off can target the booster; a poor result is a useful answer that points to offering support to everyone.
efficiency: Uses a check already completed and dates already held; about one hour of analyst time per intake.
costs: Residency coordinator and analyst time within existing roles; no participant payments.
grants: None needed; a positive result could support a nursing education grant to evaluate the booster itself.
partnerships: Residency educators, the human resources analytics team, two residents from the previous intake as advisors, and the nurses' union representative for the information sheet.
rebPath: Approved by the hospital research ethics board on 2026-07-30 (REB-2026-417) with verbal consent; the human resources release is covered by HR-DR-2026-12.
limitations: Single hospital; early leavers are not tested; the estimate is imprecise with about 56 separations.
summary: Minimal-risk accuracy study with verbal consent, scores withheld from managers, and descriptive equity reporting.
